claims.text: Over 1,300 Stripe pull requests merged each week are completely minion-produced and human-reviewed, containing no human-written code (up from 1,000 as of Part 1).

Stripe's unattended agent coding requires a cloud developer environment that is parallelizable, predictable, and isolated, so agents have clean working directories and do not interfere with one another's changes.
Minions run on the devbox, the same standard developer environment Stripe engineers use, which is an AWS EC2 instance containing Stripe's source code and running services under development.
Stripe treats devboxes as 'cattle, not pets': standardized and easy to replace rather than bespoke and long-lived.
Many Stripe engineers use one devbox per task, and an engineer might have half a dozen running at a time.
Stripe aims for a devbox to be ready within 10 seconds by proactively provisioning and warming a pool of devboxes in advance.
Devbox warm-up includes cloning gigantic git repositories, warming Bazel and type-checking caches, and starting code generation services that run continually on devboxes.
After the 10-second spin-up, a devbox is checked out to a recent copy of master across all of Stripe's main repos and is ready to run tests, type check, or start a web service.
Stripe built devboxes for human engineers long before LLM coding agents existed; their parallelism, predictability, and isolation also suit agents.

In late 2024 Stripe internally forked Block's goose coding agent and customized it to work within Stripe's LLM infrastructure, later focusing its development on the needs of minions rather than human-supervised use.
Because minions are fully unattended, the agent harness cannot rely on human-facing features such as interruptibility or human-triggered commands to start or steer a run.
Because mistakes are confined to the limited blast radius of one quarantined devbox, Stripe runs the agent with full permissions and skips confirmation prompts.
Blueprints are workflow templates in which each node is either an agentic step (an LLM coding loop) or a deterministic step that enforces constraints the AI is not allowed to decide for itself.
The test-validation step in a Blueprint is a gate the harness enforces regardless of what the model decides, rather than a request made to the model.
Stripe's blueprints alternate between deterministic steps such as linting, type checking, and CI and agentic steps where the AI reasons and writes code.
Each minion PR is validated against a subset of Stripe's battery of over 3 million tests before a human engineer reviews and merges it.
Minions run at most two CI rounds before handing the result to a human, even if failures remain.
The CI strategy is a local lint step taking under 5 seconds, then at most 2 CI rounds, with fixes auto-applied.
Minion devboxes are isolated from production and the internet for security.
Every minion PR requires human review before merge.
Minions are invoked via Slack, a CLI, web interfaces, and internal platform integrations.
Minions access nearly 500 MCP tools through Toolshed, Stripe's internal tool server; Part 1 cited more than 400.

Before the agent starts, the orchestrator deterministically pre-fetches context by scanning the prompt for links, pulling docs and ticket details, and searching code via Sourcegraph through MCP, giving agents curated tool subsets rather than all tools.

InfoQ reports minions perform best on well-defined tasks such as configuration adjustments, dependency upgrades, and minor refactoring, so the weekly PR count does not imply every PR is a large feature change.
Stripe's codebase consists of hundreds of millions of lines of code, mostly Ruby with Sorbet typing, with many homegrown libraries LLMs have not seen in training data.
